newsitem.title: GERMANY: Stony silence in German coalition after tax talks.
newsitem.headline: Stony silence in German coalition after tax talks.

text.p: Party leaders from German Chancellor Helmut Kohl's strained centre-right coalition drove off in silence after a crisis meeting on Wednesday that aimed to thrash out a deal on taxes and budget deficits.

Kohl's 14-year-old coalition of Christian Democrats (CDU) and Free Democrats (FDP) has come close to breaking point over proposals to raise some taxes to fill a widening budget gap as Bonn tries to qualify for Europe's single currency.
Coalition leaders had been expected to make a statement to the press after the meeting.
Bernd Protzner, general secretary of the Bavarian Christian Social Union (CSU), the CDU's sister party, said there was a "good discussion", but results of the meeting were not made known.
The coalition parties had entered the meeting still split over how to plug budget deficits and possible tax increases.

Kohl ally Wolfgang Schaeuble and Finance Minister Theo Waigel have proposed bringing forward to January 1, 1998, parts of the broad tax reform that it plans for 1999. This would include closing tax loopholes in order to raise revenue.

The move would also include broadening the tax base, which could open the door for raising some indirect taxes such as petrol taxes and value-added-tax to bring the tax rates in line with direct taxes. Waigel said this would not flow into the budget, but it could mean there would be no net tax cut in 1998.

But FDP leader Wolfgang Gerhardt, who is determined not to back down on the party's pledge not to raise taxes and to carry out sweeping tax cuts, said the government must separate the issue of tax reform from budget consolidation efforts.
"We have to make a strict division between the current budget difficulties and the tax reform," Gerhardt told the mass daily Bild in an interview that appeared on Wednesday.
"The earlier burdens on citizens and businesses are eased and more room for investment and jobs is created the better. Net tax cuts and striking tax exemptions go together."
Both coalition partners spread contradictory reports after a round of emergency budget meetings on Tuesday.

The FDP said the two sides had moved closer and it would be possible to resolve the current budget crisis without raising taxes this year or next. Party officials also said that plans to cut the solidarity tax, a 7.5 percent surcharge on income tax bills to finance German unity, were unchanged.
But Kohl's conservative alliance said no agreement with the junior coalition partner FDP was in sight.

Deputy CDU parliamentary leader Heiner Geissler said his party's patience with the FDP was running out. "An agreement must be found so that the euro can come on time, so that tax reform comes and so that pension reforms come and lead to lower pension contributions," Geissler told German radio.
"We can't keep going along with this for much longer, because we are not ready... to risk the trust of citizens."

German commentators interpreted Schaeuble's proposal to bring forward parts of the tax reform, which marked an about-face in the CDU's position, as the first move in an effort to win FDP support for higher petrol taxes.

But the FDP immediately rejected the idea as a "hidden tax hike" which it fears could cost it dearly in general elections next year. It went into the next round of coalition talks determined to draw a line between the budget and tax talks.
Germany's budget woes have become one of the main risks to a timely start of European economic and monetary union (EMU) in 1999.

Record unemployment and low tax revenues have torn gaping holes in the budgets for this year and next, leaving the government scrambling for new revenues and spending cuts and threatening to derail its bid to qualify for EMU.
The government aims to fill the budget gap with privatisation revenues, spending cuts and higher borrowing while still seeking to meet the tough fiscal criteria for participation in monetary union.

"The tax reform will be voted in with the coalition majority in parliament on June 26," said a confident Michael Glos, parlimentary leader of the Bavarian CSU in an article for the party newspaper BayernKurier.
